opener.heading: Week 21: Superheroes & Helpers 🦸
about: The cape comes out of an old t-shirt on Friday morning, and the other six days are the work that goes with wearing it. Azlyn cuts a shield out of a cereal box and finds out what it stops, rigs a string over a broom handle and hauls six stranded toys up off the floor, makes six foil medals and hands them over on doorsteps, gets through six hard things in a row on Monday and puts her own finger on the smoke alarm button on Tuesday. A helper in this house does something, and every day names the something.

Nothing on the calendar this week, which leaves room for two heavy days back to back. Monday is ice water, a bag of flour and a hill she walks up on her own legs. Tuesday is the loudest morning in the book. Wednesday answers both of them with a sick bay on the sofa and a bed on the living room floor with a bell beside it, and by Thursday she is sitting down sorting the whole week into a shoebox. Four things outlast the seven days: the cape and the shield, both dated, the training chart with a row on it for Kreston, the fire route map on the fridge, and the box itself, which holds the spare medal that comes back out on a doorstep later in the year.
azlyn: A symbol that stands for her. Ten scraps on the table Friday, one chosen for her back and copied big onto her shield, then the same idea again on six foil medals with wool threaded through the hole and on ten cards with a face on each.
A string over a pole lifts what her arms cannot. She pulls down and the tub goes up, and on Saturday afternoon she carries the trick outside to a bowl of water and fifteen minutes on the tongs.
Doing a hard thing she chose. Five seconds of ice, a bag of flour to the far wall and back, thirty seconds of sitting still, each one once and each one over when it is over.
Saying what is wrong before anybody fixes it. A tub that comes off the string, a shield that folds the first time it is hit, six patients with a poorly tummy, each one named out loud by her first.
Loud things she starts and stops herself. Her finger under yours on the smoke alarm button, her hand on the vacuum switch, ear defenders on because she asked for them.
you: A made thing needs a job or it stops mattering
Combining two past activities is a real cognitive step
Marking the end of something matters
Being uncomfortable on purpose is a useful experience
Understanding a frightening thing shrinks it
Sick days shrink a child's world, and that's part of what's hard
Recovery boredom is the right time for collections

Cereal boxes or thin card, 7 (the shield, the medals, the cards, the chart, the clipboard)

A hole punch, if you have one

A mug or a jar lid to draw round
Envelopes, 6, or spare paper to fold round the notes
A small box or an old envelope for the helper cards
A small plastic tub, or a second shoebox, for the lifting machine
A broom or a mop handle

A bulldog clip, or a clothespin
6 small toys, and a can of beans for the heavy load

The vacuum, and a dustpan and brush of her own

A small beaker, and a beaker with a lid
A bell, or a spoon and a mug
A bag for the roadside finds
opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 11 months this week. He lets go of the table and stands on his own for a second or two before he drops, pulls himself up on a chair leg to get there, and holds a long babbled conversation with anyone who answers. Name the thing in his hands every time he looks up at you.

days.title: The Hero She Invents
days.prepTonight: Flatten two cereal boxes onto the table with an old adult t-shirt nobody wants back, the markers, the foil and the tape.

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Shield That Matches the Cape

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Cape and the Sofa Cushions

opening.title: Ten Symbols, One Winner
opening.need: 1 sheet of paper · crayons or markers · the old t-shirt from last night.
steps: Tear the sheet into ten rough pieces and spread them on the table.
One symbol on each: a star, a bolt, a spider, whatever arrives. Draw your own beside her if she stalls.
Lay all ten out and ask which one goes on her back. The winner sits on the t-shirt until 9:15.

main.title: The Cape That Fits Her
materials: 1 old adult t-shirt or a plain pillowcase
Permanent markers, or washable poster paint and a thin brush
Her chosen symbol on paper from this morning
steps: Lay the t-shirt on the newspaper. Cut the front panel away, then both sleeves. What is left is the cape.
Hold it against her shoulders, hem at her knees, and trim the top corners so they sit flat.
Put this morning's symbol in the middle and hold it still while she copies it large in marker.
The rest of the cape is hers, including whatever runs off the edge.
Stand her up and tape both top corners to the shoulders of the t-shirt she has on, two strips a side. Nothing goes round her neck.
Write the date inside the hem in marker. She will be too tall for this by autumn.
main.tip: Tape re-does itself. When a shoulder pulls loose mid-afternoon, hand her the roll rather than taking the cape off her.

outside.title: Where the Wind Catches It
paras: Cape on, and find a long straight run: the top of the field, an empty path, the fence line down the garden. Send her one way, then back, and watch which direction lifts it. Late May gives you a warm wind most mornings, and she will find the spot where it works.

days.infant: Kreston is 11 months and stands alone for a few seconds. Spread the sleeve you cut off this morning on the grass and sit him where Azlyn's run passes close. A person going fast and then vanishing behind him beats any toy, and he twists right round to find her again.

second.title: The Shield That Matches the Cape
second.intro: The cape is on her back where she cannot see it. A shield sits out in front of her where she can, carrying the same symbol.
materials: 2 flattened cereal boxes, or one side of a bigger box
Her symbol on paper from this morning
steps: Lay the cape out with the symbol facing up. Draw the shield on one flattened box, as wide as her shoulders and no longer than her waist, and she holds the card flat while you cut.
Cut a second panel the same shape out of the other box, glue it to the back of the first, then both of you stand on it. One layer folds the first time she uses it.
Foil over the front, torn into squares, edges folded round the back and glued down. Wrinkles make it look like metal.
Her symbol goes on the foil in permanent marker, drawn big. Everything else on the front is hers.
The handle is a strip of card folded into a U, both ends taped flat to the back. Try it on her forearm and add tape until it holds when she swings it.
Then it has to work. Lob the rolled socks slow and high from across the room while she blocks. Six throws, then she throws at you.
Date the back in marker, the same date as the cape hem, and hang it on her door handle.
second.tip: Cut it smaller than she asks for. A shield wider than her shoulders drags on the floor and gets put down inside five minutes.

alternatives: Draw the shield on paper and tape it to a whole cereal box, no cutting.
Cuffs instead: two strips of card rolled round her wrists and taped.
A second shield for whoever else is in the house, and they swap symbols.
One shield, and the rest of the afternoon throwing socks at it.
outAgain: A friend's house, cape on, because it gets explained at the door
The park in the cape, and let it come home with grass on it
The corner store for more tape, since half a roll went this morning
The long way round the block, with her pointing out what is broken in the street
A café garden and something cold, if the afternoon has gone warm

aroundWorld.title: West Africa & the Caribbean: Anansi 🕷️
paras: Anansi is a spider, and in Ghana he has been the hero of hundreds of stories for centuries. He wins by being clever and never by being strong. Enslaved West Africans carried his stories across the Atlantic, and in Jamaica and Trinidad he became Anancy, still small, still winning.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Groundnut stew is a Ghanaian dinner she can help make. Stir two big spoons of peanut butter into a tomato and chicken stew until it goes thick, and serve it over rice while somebody tells an Anansi story.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: In Ghana the stories are called Anansesem, which means "spider words".

days.krestonPM: Hand him two big cardboard offcuts to bang together, the game he would pick for himself at 11 months. You press any tape down, because tape ends up in his mouth in four seconds. He pulls up on the table leg, so the scissors and the foil live at the far end.

insight.headline: A made thing needs a job or it stops mattering.
paras: Half the crafts in this house die on the table they were made on. The cape went out into the wind at half past ten and came back with grass on it. The shield had six socks thrown at it before dinner. Azlyn judges a thing she has made by whether it does what it was for, and she puts real care into the parts that carry the load once she knows what the load is. Tell her the job before she starts, then give her the job the same day. The ones that get used are the ones she rebuilds herself when they come apart.

days.safety: Heavy scissors, with Kreston at 11 months and cruising. They stay on the table and go back in the drawer the moment the cutting stops. Fasten the cape at the shoulders with tape and tie nothing round her neck. A cut cardboard edge is sharp, so run masking tape round the whole shield before she takes it off the table. Sweep the foil scraps up before he is on the floor.

days.title: The Rescue Machine
days.prepTonight: Stand two dining chairs of the same height a meter apart against a clear wall, with the broom, the string and a small tub between them.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: Stranded on the Living Room Floor

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Rescued Toys Lined Up to Dry

opening.title: Stranded on the Living Room Floor
opening.need: 6 small toys of her choosing · 1 roll masking tape.
steps: Tape a square on the floor near the chairs, big enough for all six toys, and stand them in it while she watches.
Inside the square is water and nothing comes out of it by hand. Ask her how she would get them out, then leave the problem alone.
Tell her the machine that lifts them out goes up at 9:15. An hour of walking round them is half of what makes it matter.

main.title: The Lifting Machine
materials: 1 small plastic tub or a shoebox
2 dining chairs of the same height
Small toys and a can of beans as cargo
steps: Stand the chairs back to back a meter apart against the wall. Lay the broom handle across both backs and tape it down.
Tape the string to the middle of the tub, two strips crossed over, and test it before you trust it.
Throw the free end over the handle and into her hands. She pulls down and the tub goes up. Five or six empty runs first.
Load the six toys out of the square one at a time. The bulldog clip holds each at the top while she stands back and looks.
Put the can of beans in. It takes both hands and most of her weight.
Drag one chair further out so the string runs at a slant. It still works, and it is harder.
main.tip: She will load it past what the tape holds. Let the tub come down once, and let her re-tape it herself.

outside.title: The Bins Nobody Brought In
paras: Half the street's trash carts are still at the curb from collection day. Bring in the ones belonging to houses you know, knocking first anywhere you are not sure. A cart is taller than she is and steers like a shopping cart, so she takes one side of the handle. Count them at the last drive.

days.infant: Kreston is 11 months and stands alone for a few seconds. Take him on the round facing forward and stop the stroller square in front of each bin: the wheels, the lid, the bang over the curb. Back home, the empty tub on the floor is his to fill and tip out.

second.title: The Flood on the Patio
second.intro: The machine comes outside. A dishpan of water is the flood, and everything in it is stranded.
materials: 1 large dishpan or a kiddie pool
Water, by tap or watering can
The lifting machine from this morning
steps: Rig the machine on flat ground: chairs a meter apart, handle taped across both backs, tub on the string, bowl underneath.
She fills the bowl with the watering can. Warm water from the tap beats cold water from the hose in May.
Tip the toys in and announce the flood. She takes it from there and you can stop talking.
Round one is by hand. She fishes each one out, loads the tub and hauls it up, where it counts as saved.
Round two is tongs and sieve only. Give her something only the tongs manage, like a slippery ball off the bottom.
Empty the bowl over a flower bed together and turn it upside down on the grass, before anybody heads indoors.
Dry her with one towel and mop the patio with the other, change her clothes, then untape the string and coil it away.
second.tip: Fifteen minutes of tongs is real hand strength and she thinks it is a rescue.

alternatives: One bowl, one sieve, no machine.
Wash the toys with a washcloth and a bar of soap on the step.
Rig the machine over the stairs and haul cargo up to the landing.
Run the hose down the path and float things along the gutter.
outAgain: The lakeshore, for water that does not fit in a bowl
The shady side of the park with a bottle of water
The stream at the end of the woods path, rain boots on
The garden, the sprinkler, and nothing planned
A friend's kiddie pool if anybody has one out yet
days.krestonPM: Kreston is 11 months and goes nowhere near the bowl on his own. Give him a tray of his own with a finger's depth of water in it, on the grass with you beside him. At the lakeshore he stays in your arms or in the stroller, and the brake goes on every time you stop.

insight.headline: Combining two past activities is a real cognitive step.
paras: A pulley she learned at 9:15 arrives at a problem it was never built for, and psychologists call that transfer. It is the slowest thing to teach and most of the point of teaching anything. A three-year-old who has only pulled the string in the living room has a party trick. The same child reaching for it over a bowl of water has a tool. Rig the machine within sight of the new problem and say nothing about what it is for. The connection she makes without help is the one she keeps, and she will try it on the next stuck thing she meets.

days.safety: The broom handle comes down on a head if Kreston pulls himself up on a chair leg, so rig it against a wall and stay in the room. Take the string down the moment you finish. Standing water is a drowning risk at 11 months, so tip the bowl out before you go inside, not after.

days.title: Medals for the Helpers
days.prepTonight: Flatten two or three cereal boxes onto the table with the foil, the wool and a mug to draw round, and fill the ice cube tray for tomorrow.

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: The Finish Line Across the Path

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Six Names on the Morning List

opening.title: The List of Who Helps
steps: Ask who helps her, and write every name down in her words. The garbage man counts. The dog counts.
Keep going until six of them are on the paper, then read the list back to her.
She puts them in order. That order is the order the medals get made in at 9:15, and she should hear you say so.

main.title: Foil Medals on Wool
materials: 2–3 cereal boxes or similar thin card
A mug or jar lid to draw round
steps: She holds the mug on the flattened card while you run the marker round it seven times: six for the list, one spare.
Cut the seven circles out. Adult scissors, adult hands, and say why she holds the card and not the handles.
She wraps a torn square of foil round each, folds the edges back and glues them down. Wrinkles make it look like metal.
Push the pencil through the top of each medal, on a spare piece of cereal box.
Cut the wool into seven 25 cm lengths, thread one through each hole and knot it into a loop for a wrist or a door handle.
She marks the front however she likes. You write the name on the back in marker while she watches.
main.tip: Foil tears at the fold. Wrap a second square over any medal that splits.

outside.title: The Finish Line Across the Path
paras: Every race needs a line at the end. Walk until you find one already there, a lamppost or a gate or a drain cover. Race her to it: you against her, her against you running backwards, both of you on hands and knees. Keep the line in the same place and let her lose a couple.

days.infant: Kreston is 11 months and stands alone for a couple of seconds. Stand him on the grass at the finish line facing you, let go for a count of two, then catch him. He gets the same shout Azlyn gets when she crosses. Three or four goes, then stop. The standing costs him everything he has.

second.title: The Ceremony on the Doorstep
second.intro: Six medals on a table are craft. Six handed over on a doorstep, with a note and a line said out loud, come up again the next time somebody wins something.
materials: 1 envelope or a folded sheet per note, 6
steps: Notes first. She says what each person did and you write it word for word, one sheet each.
Fold each note into an envelope, or fold a sheet round it and tape it shut. She marks the front in marker.
Rehearse: cushion as the podium, cape on, the line practiced twice. Name, what they did, then the medal.
The people in the house go first. She stands on the cushion, calls a name, and they come to her.
Tape Kreston's medal flat to the high-chair tray, where he can pat it and cannot lift it.
Doorstep round next, knocking only at doors you would knock at anyway. Where nobody is in, the note goes through and the medal comes home.
Finish with the two who never come to the door: tape one to the trash can lid and drop one inside your mail slot.
second.tip: Let her say the line wrong. A rehearsed three-year-old goes quiet and delivers the whole thing to the sidewalk, and the person hears it fine.

alternatives: Mail the medals through the doors and skip the ceremony.
Draw the six helpers instead, a page each, and keep them.
Give the medals to the soft toys and hold the whole thing indoors.
Make one enormous medal for the entire street and tape it to the gate.
outAgain: The scooter, medal still on her wrist, down the flattest path you have
The park loop, and time her round it twice
The duck pond on foot if the scooter gets abandoned at the corner
A long slow family walk with no destination in it
The school playground, empty on a Sunday and better for it
days.krestonPM: Kreston is 11 months and takes names in faster in a room where they get said out loud. Put him where he can see the ceremony and say each name clear and slow as the medal changes hands. He rides behind the scooter with his medal flat on the tray.

insight.headline: Marking the end of something matters.
paras: Azlyn has no calendar and no clock, so a stretch of work ends when somebody tells her it has ended. The medal leaves her hand, the person says something back, and the thing is finished in a way that a craft left drying on the table never manages. Rituals with a clear last moment help children file an experience as done, which is part of why birthdays carry so much weight at three. Without a last moment she carries on tinkering with the same six medals until they come apart. She made every one of them knowing where it was going, and she watched it land.

days.safety: Seven loops of wool at floor height and an 11-month-old who pulls to stand. A loop of wool over Kreston's head is a strangulation risk, so his medal is taped flat to the tray and never goes round him. The spare goes up on a shelf when the ceremony ends. The scissors stay with you.

days.title: Hero Training
days.prepTonight: The ice is in the freezer. Put the flour, the towel, the cushion and the masking tape by the table and clear the floor to the far wall.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: The Bowl of Ice on the Table

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: Six Hard Things in a Row

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: The Hill You Have to Walk Up

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Chart with a Row for Kreston

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Long Bath After the Hill

opening.title: The Bowl of Ice on the Table
opening.need: 1 mixing bowl of cold water · the tray of ice cubes · 1 towel.
steps: Bowl on the table, and she tips the ice in one cube at a time.
Both hands in for five seconds while you count out loud, then into the towel.
Ask whether she would do it again. Whatever she says, tell her that was one of six and the rest wait until 9:15.

main.title: Six Hard Things in a Row
materials: 1 bag of flour or a full 2-liter bottle as the heavy load
Masking tape for the start line
Paper and a thick marker for the tally
1 kitchen timer, or the stopwatch on your phone
steps: Tape a start line across the floor and write the six jobs down the paper in marker: ice, carry, one leg, still, slow, quiet.
Ice is already done. Put the first mark beside it on the paper before anything else starts.
The carry: the flour from the line to the far wall and back. She puts it down halfway and picks it up herself.
One leg on the cushion for as long as she lasts, timer running. Then the still one, sat on it until the timer reaches thirty seconds.
The slow walk is heel to toe from the line to the door. The long silence comes last, timer on, and she breaks first.
Tape the paper to the wall at her height and count the six marks with her.
main.tip: Each happens once. None of them are fun and all of them end, and a second go at the ice turns the morning into a dare.

outside.title: The Hill You Have to Walk Up
paras: Find the steepest thing within walking distance: a hill, a footbridge, a long flight of steps, the parking lot ramp. Walk up it. Somewhere near the top she asks to be carried. Stop, count ten breaths together, then keep going on her own legs.

days.infant: At 11 months Kreston is doing his own hard thing on the same hill. Let him out of the stroller on the flat at the top, on grass, and hold your hands a foot from his while he stands for two or three seconds. When he drops, wait and see whether he pulls himself back up on your knee.

second.title: The Chart with a Row for Kreston
second.intro: The chart goes up this afternoon and stays for the rest of the week, with a row on it that is not hers.
materials: 1 large sheet of paper, or a cereal box flattened out
1 ruler or a straight strip of card
Stickers, or half a potato cut into a stamp with poster paint
steps: Lay the paper landscape and rule six lines across it, which gives you seven rows. She holds the ruler, you draw, and swap when she asks.
Write the six jobs down the left edge in marker, one to a row, with a small drawing beside each so she can read it without you.
The seventh row is Kreston's, and standing up on his own is his hard thing. She draws him in crayon.
Rule each row into five or six boxes across.
Tape it low enough that she can reach the top row on her toes.
Tick this morning in: a sticker in each of the six boxes she earned, and one in Kreston's row.
Leave the stickers beside it. Whatever either of them does this week gets marked by the one who did it.
second.tip: Do not turn a full row into a prize. The boxes record that a thing happened, and a chart that pays out becomes work she does for you.

alternatives: One box and one sticker on the back of an envelope.
Draw round her hand and tick a finger for each job.
Chalk the chart on the patio and let the weather have it.
Run the six hard things again in the yard.
outAgain: The big slide playground, because the ladder is a hard thing with a reward on top
The green space with a ball and nothing organized
The woods path, for the fallen log she has to get over
The riverside path as far as the second bridge
Home and the sprinkler, if the hill took everything she had
days.krestonPM: At 11 months Kreston wants whatever Azlyn has got at the playground. Sit down at the bottom of the slide with him on your knee and let him catch Azlyn as she arrives, which fits Hero Training better than anything else on offer, then put him on the flat rubber to pull up on the frame. Nobody rides a slide holding a baby on their lap: his foot catches the surface, your weight carries the leg through, and that is how a shin breaks. Name the slide out loud every time Azlyn comes down it.

insight.headline: Being uncomfortable on purpose is a useful experience.
paras: Azlyn spends her day steering round things that feel bad and you spend yours helping her. The ice bowl was five seconds she agreed to, that she could have stopped, and that ended when you said it would. Chosen, brief and predictable is what turns a hard thing into a useful one, and tolerance for discomfort builds in small doses with an adult sitting beside her. The flour bag works the same way. She found out that her arms hold out longer than her opinion of them did, and she found it out on a Monday morning with a bag of flour.

days.safety: Ice water is five seconds, counted out loud, then the towel. Do not let her leave her hands in it and never hold ice against her skin. Kreston does not go near the bowl. Run the heavy carry along a cleared route with nobody sitting on the floor in it.

days.title: The Loud Things
days.prepTonight: Check which smoke alarm you can reach off the step stool, and leave the stool, the flashlight, the chalk and the ear defenders together in the hall.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Test Button She Presses Herself

opening.title: The Noise Ladder
opening.need: 1 sheet of paper · 1 marker · the noisy things in your house.
steps: Draw a ladder up the sheet with six rungs on it.
Go round the house collecting noises, one per rung: a whisper, the tap, the kettle, the vacuum, the doorbell, the smoke alarm at the top.
Tell her the top one goes off at 9:15, with her finger on the button and her ears covered. Then leave it alone.

main.title: The Test Button She Presses Herself
materials: Your smoke alarm and a step stool (adult on the stool)
Ear defenders, or a folded dish towel held over each ear
Chalk to mark the meeting spot outside
Paper and a marker for the route map
steps: Kreston goes first, to the far end of the house, held by somebody, ears covered. Nobody presses anything until that has happened.
You on the stool with Azlyn on one hip, ear defenders on, her finger on the button under yours. Count down from three.
Ask what she thought and take whatever comes back. Press it again only if she asks.
Cape on, and walk the route out: the door you would use, the spot in the street where everybody stands. Chalk a circle there.
Walk it again with the lights off and the flashlight in her hand. She leads, you follow.
Draw the map together: the front door, an arrow, the chalk circle, everybody's names in it. It goes on the fridge.
main.tip: Say what will happen, in order, then do that and nothing else. She can handle the noise.

outside.title: Listening for Sirens
paras: Walk to wherever the traffic is and find a wall to sit on. Windows are open across the street in late May and you hear more than in March. A siren might take twenty minutes. When one comes, ask whether it is getting louder or quieter, and say once that somebody is on the way to help.

days.infant: Kreston startles less than two months ago, though a siren close up still gets a whole-body flinch and then a look straight at your face. That look is him checking you, and a calm face settles him inside a second. Sit him on your knee where he can see the road.

second.title: Her Hands on the Vacuum
second.intro: The vacuum is the loudest thing in the house she is allowed to switch on, and this afternoon the switch is hers.
materials: Ear defenders or the dish towel
Masking tape to mark the route
1 dustpan and brush of her own
steps: Clear the first room together before the vacuum comes out: toys in the box, rug corners flipped back.
Tape a route across the floor, two long strips she has to follow with the head of the vacuum.
Show her the switch and put her hand on it. On, off, on, off, four times, before it moves an inch.
Ear defenders on if she wants them, then let her run the route. Carry the body of it while she steers the head.
She takes the corners the vacuum missed with her own dustpan and brush and tips them into the bin.
One sticker on the door frame of every room she finishes, and the cord goes back in the reel between rooms.
Her bedroom is last and it is her call whether it gets done.
second.tip: Let her switch it off whenever she wants. A three-year-old holding the off switch stands next to a noise for twenty minutes, and thirty seconds without it.

alternatives: Ear defenders on and the vacuum watched from the doorway.
Sweep the whole downstairs with the dustpan and brush instead.
Wipe the baseboards with a damp cloth, one room at a time.
Do one room, then spend the rest of the afternoon under a blanket.
outAgain: Swimming, and the pool is the loudest room she stands in all week
The splash pad, if it has opened for the season
Indoor playground, if the pool is shut
The park, for something quiet after a noisy day
A shady café garden and a long cold drink
days.krestonPM: The pool echo is the biggest sound Kreston meets at 11 months. Hold him chest to chest for the first few minutes with one ear against you, then turn him out to watch Azlyn. Stand him on the shallow step with your hands under his arms.

insight.headline: Understanding a frightening thing shrinks it.
paras: Azlyn has heard the smoke alarm before, in the middle of some Tuesday, for no reason she could see. It is loud, it arrives with no warning, and the no warning does most of the frightening. Today she knew it was coming, she covered her own ears, and her finger was on the button. Fear research keeps landing on the same two levers, predictability and control, and a noise she can predict and stop is a different thing from one that arrives on its own. She has the useful half of it now: that sound means everybody walks out to the chalk circle.

days.safety: A smoke alarm is rated at 85 decibels three meters away and is much louder right underneath it, which is where her head is. Ear defenders on before anybody presses anything. Kreston goes to the far end of the house with somebody holding him and his ears covered, and that happens before anyone touches the button. On your own that means the stroller at the bottom of the yard with the door shut, or moving the Main Event to a day Joseph is home. Never with him loose in the house. Check it sounds again when she has finished. Never pull the battery to make the day easier. The stool is adult only, so Azlyn goes up on your hip and never stands on it. The vacuum cord goes back in the reel. At the pool and at the splash pad stay within arm's reach of both of them, close enough to take hold without a step.

days.title: The Sick Bay
days.prepTonight: Line five or six soft toys along the sofa with the dish towels, the paper towels and a handful of craft sticks beside them.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Sick Bay on the Sofa

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Bed on the Floor with a Bell

opening.title: Wristbands for the Patients
opening.need: the 5–6 soft toys · 1 roll masking tape · 1 marker · 1 sheet of paper.
steps: Line the toys along the sofa and let her name each one out loud. Write the names down.
Tear a strip of tape for each, write the name on it, and let her wrap it loose round an arm.
Ask what is wrong with each patient and write that on the tape too, in her words. That is the 9:15 round.

main.title: The Sick Bay on the Sofa
materials: Craft sticks or clean wooden spoons as thermometers
Paper, a marker and a piece of card for a clipboard
1 lidded box for the small parts
steps: Lay each patient on its own dish towel along the sofa, heads at the same end. That row is the ward.
Tape a sheet of paper to the card and hand her the clipboard. One line per patient.
Temperature first: a craft stick under the arm, count to five, and she writes the number on the clipboard in marker.
Bandages next. Tear the paper towels into strips, wrap, and tape the end down flat. Nothing across a face, nothing tight round a limb.
Water round: the beaker goes to each mouth and comes back, one sip each, and she wipes them with the dish towel.
Big light off and the flashlight on for the last check. She decides which ones are getting better.
main.tip: Let her diagnose the same thing six times over. Every patient gets a poorly tummy. Treat the sixth one the way you treated the first.

outside.title: The Blanket Under the Tree
paras: Take a blanket to the shadiest tree you can walk to and lie down. The leaves are full in late May and the light comes through in moving patches. Bring two patients and prop them against the trunk. Ask what a poorly person needs, and let the answer be twenty minutes outside doing nothing.

days.infant: Grass in late May is a whole texture problem for Kreston at 11 months. Sit him on the edge of the blanket with one hand on the wool and one on the grass and let him work out which he prefers. Name what is under each hand while he does it.

second.title: The Bed on the Floor with a Bell
second.intro: The best part of being poorly is the bed downstairs with everything in reach. She builds one on the living room floor and rings for you.
materials: 1 small bowl and a lidded beaker
1 bell, or a spoon and a mug
steps: Build the bed together: duvet folded double for the mattress, the folded towel under the head end, two pillows on top.
Lay out what she needs down her right side, inside her reach: bowl, beaker with the lid on, tissues, flashlight, books.
She gets in and you leave the room. She rings the bell, or bangs the spoon on the mug, and you come.
Take her order and bring it without editing it: water, a book off the pile, the tissues moved four inches.
Swap over. You get in the bed and she runs the ward.
Two books read lying down, flashlight on, big light off.
Leave the bed up until dinner. She goes back into it on her own and that half hour is the best of it.
second.tip: Come every single time she rings. She is finding out that a sound she makes brings a person.

alternatives: One pillow, one blanket, one book, and stop there.
Make a get-well card for somebody who is poorly.
Bath the patients in the sink and dry them on the radiator.
Put one patient in the stroller and take it round the block.
outAgain: The library, and ask at the desk for a book about a doctor
A park bench with a book each, if the library is shut
Indoor playground, for a body that has been on the floor since one
The pharmacy, to look at the bandages and buy one box
A slow walk with the stroller and two patients in the basket
days.krestonPM: At 11 months Kreston wants the library shelf rather than the story. Let him pull board books out before you sit down. Sit him against your leg for the rhyme session, and Azlyn chooses his book.

insight.headline: Sick days shrink a child's world, and that's part of what's hard.
paras: When Azlyn is ill her world contracts to one room and two people. She loses the park, the other children, and the small landmarks that tell her what day it is, and some of what looks like misery is her world shrinking. Playing it out on a well day hands the shrinking back to her. She picks who is poorly, who gets the bell answered and when everybody is better, and she gets to be the one arriving with the water. Children rehearse the parts of life they have no say in, and the rehearsal works long before the next temperature turns up.

days.safety: Do not hand her real medicine bottles, empty syringes or old blister packs as props. A three-year-old who has practiced dosing a teddy from a real syringe will do it for real when nobody is watching. A clean spoon and water do the same job. The bell and the craft sticks are choke-sized and go back in the box before Kreston is on the floor, and no tape goes tight round a finger or across a face.

days.title: The Helper Cards
days.prepTonight: Flatten a cereal box onto the table with the scissors, a pencil and a ruler, and dig out the shoebox and two or three photos of people she knows.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: A Card for Everyone Who Turns Up

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Box the Whole Week Goes In

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Box Goes Beside the Bed

opening.title: Ten Cards the Same Size
opening.need: 1 flattened cereal box · 1 pair of scissors (adult only) · 1 pencil · 1 ruler or a straight strip of card.
steps: Rule the flattened box into ten rectangles about the size of your hand. She holds the straight edge, you draw.
Cut them out yourself while she counts them into a stack. Keep the offcuts.
Ten cards, ten people. Ask who the first is for and leave the stack squared up.

main.title: A Card for Everyone Who Turns Up
materials: The ten cut cards from this morning
1 marker for you to write her words down
2–3 photos she can copy a face from
1 old envelope or a small box
steps: One card, one person, and she says the name before she draws. Start with whoever she is surest about.
She draws the face on the front in crayon and marker. Set a photo beside her for the ones she asks help with.
Turn it over and ask what that person is good at. Write it on the back in marker, word for word: he fixes the car.
Punch a hole in the top corner of each finished card, or push the pencil through on this morning's offcuts.
Stickers on whichever ones she wants them on.
All ten go into the envelope or the small box, counted in by name.
main.tip: Write her words down and not the tidy version. She gives me the crusts is the line that makes the person at the door laugh.

outside.title: Ten Things Off the Roadside
paras: The roadsides are at their loudest in the last week of May: buttercups, white and red clover, wild mustard gone over to yellow, the first ox-eye daisies, dandelion clocks half blown. Take a bag and pick ten things, one at a time, and let her choose all ten. Stay on the roadside and off anybody's garden, leave anything tall and lacy alone, and wash both pairs of hands at the door.

days.infant: Kreston pulls up on the wheel arch of the stroller now, which means whatever he grabs goes in his mouth from a new height. Hand him one of the widest leaves she picked, too big to get into his mouth, and stay next to him while he decides what it is. Name it for him while he turns it over, the same word every time.

second.title: The Box the Whole Week Goes In
second.intro: Everything the week made is on a different surface in a different room. It goes into one shoebox this afternoon.
materials: The spare medal and the training chart
steps: Stand the thick card up inside the box and mark where it needs cutting. You cut the dividers, she holds the box.
Tape each divider upright with masking tape down both sides. She chooses how wide the sections are.
She says what goes in each. Write it on the divider in marker: cards, flowers, medals, paper.
Tape the flattest roadside finds to a spare piece of card with clear tape, then lay that in its section.

Load the rest: the helper cards counted in by name, the spare medal with its wool cut off, and the training chart folded in half. Tuesday's route map stays on the fridge, because a fire route in a box is no route at all.
She decorates the lid in crayon. You write today's date on it in marker.
Lid on, and she takes one thing out and puts it back. That is what dividers are for and she will do it eleven times.
second.tip: Let her put things in that you would not. A stone, a bus ticket and half a cookie belong in there if she says so.

alternatives: One box, no dividers, everything in.
Photograph each thing and make a page of the week instead.
Give the helper cards out this afternoon rather than keeping them.
Sort the roadside finds by color along the windowsill and stop there.
outAgain: The garden center, one plant, chosen by her and carried by her
The hardware store, for a box with a lid that fits better
The bakery, and she hands over the money
The post office, to send one helper card to somebody far away
The park on the way home, if the cart round went well
days.krestonPM: At 11 months Kreston stays in the cart seat, strapped in, with something of his own to hold. A garden center is the best-smelling place he goes all month. Push him down the aisles slow enough to look up at the tall plants.

insight.headline: Recovery boredom is the right time for collections.
paras: By Thursday of a week like this one, Azlyn's body has had enough and her attention has not. That gap is where sorting lives. A box with dividers in it asks nothing physical of her and everything of the part of her that has spent six days working out which thing is which. She also handles every object from the week one more time, which is how a run of separate days turns into one thing she can tell somebody about. Put the box where she can reach it, then leave it alone for two weeks. She re-sorts it on the afternoons when nothing else appeals.

days.safety: A garden center stacks slug pellets, plant food, bulbs and seed packets at exactly Kreston's height, and half the display plants are poisonous if chewed. Keep him in the cart seat rather than walking the aisles, and wash both pairs of hands before anybody eats in the café. The scissors stay with you.
